extracted.intended_audience: organizers and stakeholders of the MER Forum; research mathematicians, mathematics educators, and education reform researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the MER (Mathematicians and Education Reform) Forum's effectiveness in fostering communication, collaboration, individual pedagogical change, departmental and systemic reform using survey data and qualitative comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitating communication among mathematicians about educational issues
rubrics_metrics.description: MER primarily is interested in facilitating communication among mathematicians about educational issues (i.e., communication within the mathematics community). The 1993 MER funding proposal clearly states that MER’s primary goal is to support research mathematicians as they engage in educational reform activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether MER brings together research mathematicians to discuss teaching and educational issues; evidence includes attendance of research-oriented higher education mathematicians, participant comments that MER reaches mathematicians who do not participate in other education organizations, and whether MER is perceived as a unique forum for university-level instructors to discuss teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attracting research mathematicians / uniqueness of participant mix
rubrics_metrics.description: The types of people brought together by the MER Forum was clearly its most unique aspect. The majority of comments felt MER attracts a different subset of professionals because it involves traditionally research-oriented higher education mathematics departments in K-12 mathematics education reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure uniqueness by whether MER reaches research mathematicians who otherwise would not engage with math education organizations; use participant testimony and attendance/representation data as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration between mathematicians and mathematics educators (cross-community collaboration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaboration between math and education departments would be an important advance in communications. MER seems to have some interest in fostering collaboration between mathematicians and educators (i.e., collaboration across communities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess familiarity with mathematics education literature, frequency of consulting mathematics educators for reform research, and frequency of formal/informal collaboration (e.g., once or twice each semester). Look at survey percentages (e.g., 40% consult educational research literature; two-thirds collaborate at least once or twice each semester) and qualitative comments about cross-community belonging and perceived barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with mathematics education literature / consultation of educational research
rubrics_metrics.description: I usually consult literature in the field of educational research for information about mathematics education reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-report survey items (strongly disagree → strongly agree) to measure how often participants consult educational research literature; compare across mathematicians, math-educators, and K-12 respondents to gauge cross-disciplinary uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consulting mathematics educators for reform research
rubrics_metrics.description: I usually consult mathematics educators for research about mathematics education reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure self-reported tendency to consult practitioners/education researchers; use this as an indicator of cross-disciplinary networking and whether MER reduces 'recreating the wheel' by mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collegial interactions and network-building (comfort contacting colleagues)
rubrics_metrics.description: After participating in one MER workshop, I felt comfortable calling/contacting MER colleagues I had just met about professional matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure degree of comfort (strongly disagree → strongly agree) and frequency of subsequent contacts about professional matters. Use follow-up frequency categories (never, once, 2–5 times, 6–10 times, more than 10 times) across topics (personal teaching issues, mathematics education reform issues, mathematical research issues) to quantify network effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of collaboration with educators on one's own campus
rubrics_metrics.description: How often do you formally or informally collaborate with educators in education departments on your own campus? (Never; Once/year; Once or twice/semester; Once or twice/month; More than 2 times/month)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reported frequency categories to assess local cross-department collaboration; interpret higher frequency as stronger bridge-building and potential for broader departmental change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involvement in specific types of reform activities (involvement dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Please indicate the extent of your involvement in the following: Programs for in-service teachers; Involvement with specific groups of K-12 students; Reform efforts at the school district level; Reform efforts from statewide initiatives. (Response scale: Not at all; A little; Considerably; Very)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each listed item as a separate dimension of practitioner involvement; use the four-point scale to quantify depth of engagement across levels (classroom, district, statewide, professional development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual awareness of educational issues
rubrics_metrics.description: I am more aware of the issues in mathematics education reform as a result of the MER Forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use survey agreement levels to measure enhanced awareness (e.g., >70% of mathematicians reported increased awareness). Analyze open-ended responses to identify which issues awareness increased for (calculus reform, technology, teacher preparation, diversity, state initiatives, pedagogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive atmosphere for educational reform (community support)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Forum creates a supportive atmosphere for educational reform activities, helping participants feel less isolated and more connected to colleagues to share ideas, problems, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether participation increased perceived support (e.g., willingness to contact MER colleagues about professional matters, qualitative comments about feeling less isolated). Use percentages reporting comfortable contact and examples of network support as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in classroom pedagogy attributable to MER
rubrics_metrics.description: I have changed my own teaching because I have been involved with MER. (Items also ask whether changes can be attributed to MER workshops, newsletters/publications, or networking.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure self-reported pedagogical change (agree/strongly agree), and attribute changes to specific MER sources (workshops, publications, networking). Document types of pedagogical changes (cooperative learning, technology use, hands-on activities, alternative assessments, increased student explanation/justification) provided in qualitative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection on teaching philosophy and attention to marginalized students
rubrics_metrics.description: Some mathematicians found MER to be the impetus for reflection on their teaching philosophy and on issues of students who traditionally have been marginalized by mathematics instruction, specifically women and underrepresented ethnic minorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use participant comments and survey data about reflective changes to evaluate whether MER fosters attention to equity and inclusive pedagogical philosophy; include examples and proportion of respondents reporting such reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic reform (Jenness & Barley definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systemic reform is characterized by (1) development of new or reformulation of existing systems rather than simply conducting new programs or activities, (2) the engagement of key partners in effective relationships to promote change, and (3) the identification of new roles and relationships for all players inside and outside the educational system, plus related attributes (building infrastructure, revising system elements, long-term evolving process, addressing all dimensions, building capacities, mainstreaming reform, focusing on lessons learned, placing power in hands of those in the system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this multi-attribute definition as the rubric to judge whether MER influences systemic change. Examine evidence of new working relationships, broad community-level changes (beyond individual/local), infrastructure-building, sustained initiatives, and redistribution of roles/power. The evaluators adopt this definition to judge MER’s effectiveness in influencing systemic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of broader departmental/organizational change
rubrics_metrics.description: Broader changes include changes within mathematics departments, between math and education departments on campuses, with campus administrators, and/or new involvement in large-scale educational reform projects (e.g., increased departmental support, curricular improvements, more positive attitudes toward education reform).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure departmental attitudes (items about whether reform is valued, accepted, supported), reports of new projects/programs supported in past five years, and qualitative examples (seminars, grants, colloquia) to infer organizational-level impact; account for external factors that may also drive change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary indicators of positive departmental attitude changes — Improvements in curricula
rubrics_metrics.description: One primary indicator of positive departmental attitude change toward mathematics education reform is improvements in curricula (e.g., adoption of Harvard Calculus, development of entry-level and graduate courses focused on pedagogy, remedial education reform, pre-service program rewrites).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document curricular revisions and adoption of reformed curricula as measurable signs of departmental change; use specific examples from respondents and institutional records where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary indicators of positive departmental attitude changes — New institutional support
rubrics_metrics.description: A second primary indicator is new institutional support (e.g., departmental backing for new education projects, seminars on teaching/learning, administrative invitations to speak on reform, improved ability to cite peer institutions to administration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess funding, program support, administrative recognition, and formal institutional endorsements as evidence of growing institutional commitment to mathematics education reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary indicators of positive departmental attitude changes — Attention to better pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: A third primary indicator is increased attention to better pedagogy (e.g., seminars, increased use of technology, more hands-on or participatory classroom practices, alternative assessments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure adoption of pedagogical practices, attendance at pedagogy-focused events, and reported changes in departmental norms around teaching as evidence of this indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop composition and targeting for cross-community engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: MER workshops are often either targeted toward research mathematicians or mathematics educators (K-12 and up) but not both groups at the same workshop; organizing workshops that attract a cross-section could better foster cross-community connections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate workshop participant composition, presence of sessions designed for K-12 vs. higher-education audiences, inclusion of educators as organizers/panelists, and whether workshops intentionally create break-out sessions or panels that include K-12 voices as a metric of MER’s success in promoting cross-community collaboration.
